The microwave phonon stimulated emission (SE) has been experimentally and numerically investigated in a nonautonomous microwave acoustic quantum generator, called also microwave phonon laser or phaser (see previous works arXiv:cond-mat/0303188 ; arXiv:cond-mat/0402640 ; arXiv:nlin.CG/0703050) Phenomena of branching and long-time refractority (absence of the reaction on the external pulses) for deterministic chaotic and regular processes of SE were observed in experiments with various levels of electromagnetic pumping. At the pumping level growth, the clearly depined increasing of the number of coexisting SE states has been observed both in real physical experiments and in computer simulations. This confirms the analytical estimations of the branching density in the phase space. The nature of the refractority of SE pulses is closely connected with the pointed branching and reflects the crises of strange attractors, i.e. their collisions with unstable periodic components of the higher branches of SE states in the nonautonomous microwave phonon laser.

outputs.L1: Microwave phonon stimulated emission (SE) has been investigated experimentally and numerically in a nonautonomous microwave acoustic quantum generator, also known as a microwave phonon laser or phaser (see previous works: arXiv:cond-mat/0303188; arXiv:cond-mat/0402640; arXiv:nlin.CG/0703050). Experiments conducted at various levels of electromagnetic pumping revealed branching and long-term refractority—the absence of a response to external pulses—in both deterministic chaotic and regular SE processes. As the pumping level increased, a clearly defined increase in the number of coexisting SE states was observed in both physical experiments and computer simulations. These findings confirm analytical estimates of the branching density in phase space. The refractority of SE pulses is closely associated with this branching and reflects crises of strange attractors—namely, their collisions with unstable periodic components of higher branches of SE states in the nonautonomous microwave phonon laser.
outputs.L2: Microwave-phonon stimulated emission (SE) has been studied experimentally and numerically in a nonautonomous microwave acoustic quantum generator, also known as a microwave phonon laser or phaser (see earlier studies: arXiv:cond-mat/0303188, arXiv:cond-mat/0402640, and arXiv:nlin.CG/0703050). Experiments conducted at different electromagnetic pumping intensities revealed branching and prolonged refractoriness—the failure to respond to external pulses—in both deterministic chaotic and regular SE regimes. As the pumping level increased, the number of coexisting SE states rose markedly, a result observed in physical experiments as well as computer simulations. These findings support analytical estimates of branching density in phase space. The refractoriness of SE pulses is directly associated with this branching and reflects crises of strange attractors, namely their collisions with unstable periodic components belonging to higher branches of SE states in the nonautonomous microwave phonon laser.
outputs.L3:
Microwave phonon stimulated emission was investigated both experimentally and numerically in a nonautonomous microwave phonon laser, commonly referred to as a phaser. The study focused on the system’s nonlinear dynamics under time-dependent excitation and examined how its stimulated-emission behavior changed across a range of electromagnetic pumping levels.

The experiments revealed pronounced branching and long-term refractoriness in both chaotic and regular stimulated-emission regimes. As the pumping level increased, the number of coexisting emission states rose substantially, demonstrating that stronger excitation produces an increasingly complex phase-space structure. Physical measurements and computer simulations showed close agreement with analytical estimates of the density of these branches in phase space.

The observed refractoriness of stimulated-emission pulses appears to be intrinsically connected to this branching behavior. In particular, it is associated with crises of strange attractors that occur when they collide with unstable periodic components belonging to higher branches of the emission-state hierarchy. These interactions reorganize the system’s dynamics and can temporarily suppress subsequent emission pulses, thereby producing extended refractory intervals. Overall, the results establish a close relationship among multistability, attractor crises, branching, and long-term refractoriness in the nonlinear dynamics of a driven phaser.
outputs.L4:
Microwave phonon–stimulated emission was investigated experimentally and numerically in a nonautonomous phonon laser subjected to electromagnetic pumping of variable intensity. Particular attention was paid to the complex temporal structure of the emitted phonon pulses, including the coexistence of regular and chaotic regimes, the branching of dynamical states, and the appearance of unusually long refractory intervals during which new emission pulses were temporarily suppressed.

As the pump level increased, the system exhibited a growing number of coexisting emission states associated with different branches of its nonlinear phase space. Numerical simulations reproduced the principal experimental observations and supported theoretical estimates of the number and organization of these branches. The results indicate that stronger pumping enlarges the accessible region of phase space, allowing the laser to switch among multiple stable, metastable, and chaotic patterns of stimulated phonon emission.

The long refractory periods observed in both chaotic and nominally regular pulse sequences were found to have a common dynamical origin. They arise near crises of strange attractors, when a chaotic trajectory collides with unstable periodic states located on higher emission branches. Such collisions reorganize the attractor and can force the system to spend extended intervals near weakly unstable or nearly inaccessible regions of phase space before normal pulsing resumes. Consequently, the refractory behavior is not merely a consequence of slow recovery in the active medium; it reflects global bifurcations and interactions among coexisting nonlinear states.

Overall, the agreement between experiment and numerical modeling confirms that branching, multistability, and attractor crises are central to the dynamics of a strongly pumped nonautonomous phonon laser. These findings provide a unified explanation for the proliferation of emission regimes and for the exceptionally long pauses that interrupt both chaotic and regular stimulated-phonon pulse trains.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a concise abstract about experimental and numerical studies of stimulated microwave phonon emission in a nonautonomous phaser, emphasizing branching, long-time refractoriness, pumping-level effects, and strange-attractor crises. Cite arXiv:cond-mat/0303188, cond-mat/0402640, and nlin.CG/0703050.
counterfactuals.output: **Abstract—** Experimental and numerical studies of a periodically driven microwave phonon laser (phaser) reveal complex self-organization of stimulated acoustic emission. Near resonance between pump modulation and intrinsic relaxation oscillations, the emission spectrum undergoes branching into multiple components, followed by anomalously long refractory intervals during which spectral evolution is strongly suppressed. Small variations of the pumping level can sharply alter branch structure, drift direction, and recovery time, demonstrating extreme parametric sensitivity. Nonlinear dynamical models reproduce these effects and associate abrupt transitions and prolonged transients with crises and restructuring of strange attractors in the nonautonomous spin–phonon system. These results establish phasers as experimentally accessible platforms for studying nonequilibrium branching, refractoriness, and crisis-induced dynamics [arXiv:cond-mat/0303188; arXiv:cond-mat/0402640; arXiv:nlin.CG/0703050].
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the observed chaotic and regular stimulated-emission dynamics in a microwave acoustic quantum generator, including how increased electromagnetic pumping affects the number of coexisting emission states.
counterfactuals.output:
The microwave acoustic quantum generator showed strongly nonlinear stimulated-emission behavior. Depending on operating conditions, its phonon output could settle into regular stationary or periodic regimes, or display irregular, aperiodic fluctuations and abrupt switching characteristic of deterministic chaos. Multiple stable emission patterns could exist under the same external conditions, with the realized state depending on the system’s history and perturbations.

Increasing the electromagnetic pump did not merely raise the output intensity: it increased the degree of multistability. More acoustic modes and stable emission states became simultaneously possible, producing an increasingly complex set of coexisting regular and chaotic attractors.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a research-paper abstract explaining why stimulated-emission pulses in a microwave phonon laser can become refractory to external pulses and relate this behavior to branching in phase space and collisions of strange attractors with unstable periodic states.
counterfactuals.output: We investigate the refractory response of stimulated-emission pulses in a microwave-driven phonon laser subjected to external perturbations. Experiments and nonlinear dynamical modeling show that, after a sufficiently strong emission burst, the system may temporarily fail to respond to subsequent pulses even though population inversion has substantially recovered. This behavior is therefore not explained by gain depletion alone. Instead, it arises from branching of trajectories in the phase space formed by the inversion, phonon-field amplitude, and medium polarization. External pulses can direct the system into distinct basins or weakly connected regions of a multibranch strange attractor, including trajectories that remain near low-emission states for anomalously long times. As control parameters are varied, these attractor branches approach and collide with unstable periodic states and their invariant manifolds, producing crisis-like reorganizations of the accessible phase space. The resulting transient trapping, intermittency, and reduced susceptibility to forcing appear experimentally as a refractory interval. This framework connects pulse suppression and delayed re-excitation to global bifurcations rather than solely to microscopic relaxation times, and provides testable predictions for the dependence of refractoriness on pulse phase, amplitude, detuning, and repetition rate. The results suggest a general mechanism for history-dependent excitability in driven phonon lasers and related nonlinear wave-generation systems.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe the experimental and computational evidence for state branching in a nonautonomous microwave phonon laser, and explain how the results confirm analytical estimates of branching density.
counterfactuals.output:
In the experiment the “nonautonomous” phonon laser—a microwave-pumped ruby acoustic Fabry–Perot oscillator—was made nonautonomous by periodically modulating the pump. The control parameters were mainly the modulation frequency and depth, while the stimulated-acoustic-emission intensity was monitored mode by mode and in time.

### Experimental evidence

State branching was inferred from three related observations:

- **Several reproducible emission regimes occurred at the same external parameters.** Depending on the initial condition and on whether the modulation frequency was approached from above or below, the phaser settled into different periodic or quasiperiodic pulse sequences.
- **Frequency sweeps produced hysteresis and abrupt jumps.** A branch could be followed continuously over part of the sweep and then disappear, whereupon the system jumped to another stable regime. Reverse sweeps followed a different sequence of states.
- **Successive daughter states differed by an integer number of small relaxation oscillations, or acoustic bursts, within one modulation period.** Thus the states were not random fluctuations of output power; they formed an ordered family indexed by an integer winding or pulse number. Repeated measurements gave the same branch structure, whereas noise mainly selected which allowed branch was reached.

Time traces, spectra, and stroboscopic plots therefore showed a splitting of one response state into many coexisting phase-locked responses. Near the relevant nonlinear resonance the number of observable branches increased rapidly and the transients became very long, as expected near folds of stable periodic solutions.

### Computational evidence

The observations were reproduced by numerically integrating the periodically forced balance equations for the phonon intensity and the population inversion—the class-B-laser equations adapted to the three-level spin–phonon system. With a modulated pump, these equations constitute a nonlinear slow–fast system.

Numerical frequency sweeps and Poincaré sections showed:

- multiple stable limit cycles for one set of parameters;
- saddle-node creation and destruction of pairs of periodic states;
- hysteretic transitions between branches;
- branches distinguished by the number of relaxation excursions per forcing period;
- long-lived transients and enhanced sensitivity close to branch boundaries.

Continuation or repeated integrations from different initial conditions recovered stable branches that a single forward sweep would miss. The calculated bifurcation diagrams and output waveforms had the same ordering and qualitative spacing as the experimental diagrams. Adding realistic noise changed the probability of occupying a branch but did not remove the underlying deterministic multistability.

### Agreement with the analytical branching-density estimate

The analytical treatment reduces the slow–fast equations to a return map. During one modulation period the phaser accumulates a relaxation phase

\[
\Phi(\mu)=\int_0^{T_m}\Omega_{\rm rel}\!\left[n(t;\mu),J(t;\mu)\right]dt ,
\]

where \(\mu\) denotes the swept control parameter. Neighboring states differ by one additional \(2\pi\) turn—or, equivalently, by one additional relaxation pulse. The local number of branches per unit control-parameter interval is therefore estimated by

\[
\rho(\mu)\equiv \frac{dN}{d\mu}
   \simeq \frac{1}{2\pi}
   \left|\frac{d\Phi}{d\mu}\right|.
\]

In the experimentally relevant slow-modulation limit this is often written as a phase-counting estimate involving the recovery or transient time,

\[
N \simeq \frac{\Phi}{2\pi}
   \sim f_m\,\tau_{\rm rec},
\qquad
\rho \sim \left|\frac{d(f_m\tau_{\rm rec})}{d\mu}\right|.
\]

The measured and computed branch counts increased where the recovery time and accumulated phase increased, and the spacing between adjacent branches followed the inverse of this predicted density. Within experimental resolution and the uncertainty of the material relaxation parameters, both the observed and numerically generated numbers of branches in a given sweep interval agreed with the analytical phase-counting estimate.

Thus the conclusion rests on three mutually consistent results: direct multistability and hysteresis in the phonon-laser output, the same branching in deterministic simulations, and quantitative branch counts consistent with the analytical estimate based on one extra relaxation-phase turn per daughter state.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a technical paragraph, in the style of a translated physics abstract, on deterministic chaos, refractoriness, and attractor crises in microwave phonon stimulated emission, referencing the authors’ previous arXiv studies.
counterfactuals.output: In continuation of our previous arXiv studies devoted to nonlinear microwave phonon stimulated emission in an autonomous phaser generator, we investigate the formation of deterministic chaos under variation of pumping and resonator detuning. It is shown that the observed irregular pulsations are governed not only by the standard instability of stationary stimulated emission, but also by a pronounced refractory stage caused by slow recovery of the active-spin population inversion. Near the boundary of a periodic regime, collisions of a chaotic attractor with an unstable invariant set produce interior and boundary attractor crises, accompanied by abrupt enlargement of the oscillation amplitude, intermittency, and long transient processes. The crisis-induced dynamics demonstrates anomalously large refractory times and extreme sensitivity to weak perturbations, while remaining deterministic within the reduced balance-equation description. These results extend the scenarios considered in our earlier arXiv works and indicate that the hierarchy of spin, phonon, and resonator relaxation times is the principal factor determining chaotic microwave phonon generation.
